content: 1. The efficacy of viral suppression and recovery of CD4 cell count with the 4R regimen is equivalent to that of efavirenz. 2. Rifampicin can reduce the plasma concentrations of several antiretroviral drugs, including atazanavir, darunavir, fosamprenavir, lopinavir, saquinavir, and tipranavir. 3. Rifampicin should not be co-administered with the combination of saquinavir/ritonavir. 4. A critical contraindication is the use of rifampicin with protease inhibitors (PIs). 5. The decision to use the 4R regimen in people living with HIV (PLHIV) on antiretroviral therapy (ARVs) requires expertise in the clinical management of HIV. 6. Clinical trials have demonstrated that the 4R regimen is safe for use in children aged 0–17 years as a preventive treatment for tuberculosis (TB). 7. Rifampicin is generally considered safe for use during pregnancy. 8. In candidates for organ transplantation or anti-TNF treatment, completing latent TB infection (LTBI) treatment quickly is particularly important, making the 4R regimen advantageous over longer treatment courses. 9. For homeless individuals and prisoners being released from detention, the shorter duration of the 4R regimen may be more suitable due to limited opportunities for follow-up. 10. Women of childbearing age using oral or injectable contraceptives may need to consider non-hormonal methods of birth control during 4R treatment due to potential drug-drug interactions. 11. Opiate users on methadone replacement therapy may also be at risk of drug-drug interactions with rifampicin. 12. Concurrent use of alcohol should be avoided during treatment with rifampicin. 13. The 4R regimen can be offered to individuals eligible for LTBI treatment regardless of the TB burden in their setting. 14. The 4R regimen should not only be considered as an alternative to the 9H regimen but also in broader circumstances for individuals requiring LTBI treatment. 15. The choice of LTBI treatment regimen should consider factors such as age, drug susceptibility, risk of toxicity or interactions, co-morbidities, availability, and patient preferences. 16. Translation of trial findings into programmatic realities is critical for effective implementation. 17. Rifampicin has been well-tolerated in clinical trials, and the 4R regimen has demonstrated a favorable safety profile compared to longer regimens. 18. Individuals receiving LTBI treatment should be monitored monthly by healthcare providers, who should explain the disease process, the rationale for treatment, and the importance of completing the regimen. 19. Patients should be advised to contact their healthcare provider immediately if they experience symptoms such as anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, persistent fatigue, dark-colored urine, pale stools, or jaundice. 20. If a healthcare provider cannot be consulted, patients should stop treatment immediately upon the onset of such symptoms. 21. Monitoring should focus on liver function, particularly to prevent drug-induced hepatotoxicity. 22. Baseline liver function testing is not required for all individuals starting LTBI treatment but is encouraged for those with risk factors such as a history of liver disease, regular alcohol use, chronic liver disease, HIV infection, age >35 years, pregnancy, or the postpartum period. 23. For individuals with abnormal baseline liver function tests, clinical judgment is required to assess whether the benefits of treatment outweigh the risks. 24. Adherence to the full course of LTBI treatment is a critical determinant of clinical benefit and programmatic success. 25. The shorter duration of the 4R regimen increases the likelihood of treatment completion. 26. Interventions to enhance adherence and completion of treatment should be tailored to the specific needs of at-risk groups and the local context. 27. Concerns about adherence should not prevent the use of preventive treatment. 28. The WHO 2017 guidelines for drug-susceptible TB treatment propose several interventions to support adherence, which can also be applied to LTBI treatment. 29. An electronic application for mobile phones has been developed by WHO to guide national programs on critical data collection along the LTBI care pathway. 30. Collecting information on the occurrence of active TB in individuals who have received 4R or other LTBI treatments would be beneficial. 31. Monitoring for the emergence of drug resistance in individuals who develop TB after 4R treatment or during LTBI treatment is important. 32. Research priorities include gathering more evidence on the performance of 4R in populations with limited data, such as adults and children with HIV on ARVs and pregnant individuals. 33. Future trials should compare the safety and effectiveness of 4R with other regimens under different conditions and populations. 34. Studies should assess the durability of the effect of 4R in various settings and the potential for resistance development with different LTBI regimens. 35. Implementation research should address context-specific barriers and facilitators for 4R at the program level, including acceptability, feasibility, equity, and resource use. 36. Pharmacokinetics of rifampicin with other medicines in adults and children should be further studied. 37. Cost-effectiveness analyses should incorporate parameters from both highand low-resource settings. 38. The 4R regimen has been previously recommended by WHO for low-incidence settings. 39. Safer and more effective LTBI regimens that are easier to implement will play a critical role in reducing global TB incidence. 40. Scaling up LTBI treatment worldwide is essential to achieving the goals of the WHO End TB Strategy.
